name: Sinaugoro
catalog_quote: 1.2.1.4.1 Stress and pitch on words. On one- to three-syllable words stress and high pitch is on the first syllable. ... On words with four syllables the first and penultimate syllable is stressed. However, the stress on the first syllable is stronger. ... 1.2.1.4.2 Stress and pitch on words in a phrase. Stress and high pitch of an isolated word can change when it occurs in a phrase: ['ka.ra da.'…

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, WORD domain, rule 10 100 1010 10010...: primary initial, secondary penult from four syllables up) rests on the standard reference grammar, Tauberschmidt 1999 PL C-143, which we hold as an open PDF with text layer; the deciding passage was confirmed verbatim at pp.10-11, including five-syllable verb words showing the 10010 shape. Glottolog 5.1 lists only two descriptive works; the full local Glottolog bib (18 entries) has no phonology article, OPD, JIPA piece or dissertation, and Dutton 1970:883 (fetched sources) confirms nothing on Sinagoro phonology predates these. The one refinement found: Kolia 1975:109 (fetched sources, open PL C-29) gives the Balawaia dialect penultimate stress in words of three or more syllables (go'gome) against Tauberschmidt's initial stress on Saroa trisyllables; this is a different dialect in a one-sentence sketch remark and does not outrank

sources.citation: Kolia, John A. 1975. A Balawaia grammar sketch and vocabulary. In T.E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in languages of central and south-east Papua, 107-226. Pacific Linguistics C-29. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: 'Stress is unmarked but always occurs on the first syllable of bisyllabic words and on the second last syllable of words of more than two syllables, e.g. 'ɣoɣo many, go'gome yam (sp.), 'ɣoɣo lelevagi very many.' (Balawaia dialect, Tauruba village.)
sources.note: Second Glottolog descriptive source; its p.109 stress remark for the Balawaia dialect (penultimate in words of 3+ syllables, initial in disyllables) differs from Tauberschmidt's Saroa-dialect trisyllables ['vo.vo.ka]; worth a dialect-variation caution line on the record, not a recode.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom E. 1970. Notes on the languages of the Rigo area of the Central District of Papua. In S.A. Wurm & D.C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, 879-983. Pacific Linguistics C-13. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: No stress statement for Sinagoro; p.883: 'Indeed no statement of the phonology of Sinagoro has ever been published although several books have been printed in the language using an orthography which appears to be nearly phonemic.'
sources.locator: p.883 (survey intro); stress remarks at pp.~889, 916-917 concern Hula and the non-Austronesian Kwalean/Manubaran languages, not Sinagoro
sources.note: Survey Tauberschmidt cites for the dialect list; checked for any earlier stress statement -- none for Sinagoro (explicitly says no phonology published). No further value for the stress coding.
